claim: Asprosin is a new glucogenic and centrally acting orexigenic hormone.
source: Recently, we discovered a new glucogenic and centrally acting orexigenic hormone – asprosin.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a discovery by the authors.

claim: Asprosin is elevated in metabolic syndrome (MS) patients.
source: Asprosin is elevated in metabolic syndrome (MS) patients
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Genetic loss of asprosin results in reduced appetite, leanness, and blood glucose burden, leading to protection from MS.
source: its genetic loss results in reduced appetite, leanness, and blood glucose burden, leading to protection from MS.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by previous research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Anti-asprosin mAbs from three distinct species lowered appetite and body weight in three independent MS mouse models.
source: Anti-asprosin mAbs from three distinct species lowered appetite and body weight, and reduced blood glucose in a dose-dependent and epitope-agnostic fashion in three independent MS mouse models
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Anti-asprosin mAbs reduced blood glucose in a dose-dependent and epitope-agnostic fashion in three independent MS mouse models.
source: Anti-asprosin mAbs from three distinct species lowered appetite and body weight, and reduced blood glucose in a dose-dependent and epitope-agnostic fashion in three independent MS mouse models
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by dose-response data in Figure 2.

claim: The IC50 of anti-asprosin mAbs is approximately 1.5 mg/kg.
source: with an IC50 of ~1.5 mg/kg
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and calculated from dose-response experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: The anti-asprosin mAbs displayed a half-life of over 3 days in vivo.
source: The mAbs displayed a half-life of over 3days in vivo
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacokinetic data in Figure 6e-g.

claim: The anti-asprosin mAbs have equilibrium dissociation-constants in picomolar to low nanomolar range.
source: with equilibrium dissociation-constants in picomolar to low nanomolar range
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by binding affinity measurements in Figure 6h-j.

claim: Anti-asprosin mAbs are dual-effect pharmacologic therapy that targets two key pillars of MS – over-nutrition and hyperglycemia.
source: We demonstrate that anti-asprosin mAbs are dual-effect pharmacologic therapy that targets two key pillars of MS – over-nutrition and hyperglycemia.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study results.

claim: Obesity and its co-morbidities affect nearly a quarter of the world population.
source: Obesity and its co-morbidities, such as insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, are omnipresent, affecting nearly a quarter of the world population by some estimates (Saklayen, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: MS currently exists as an untreatable malady despite decades of basic research and drug development.
source: As a whole, MS currently exists as an untreatable malady despite decades of basic research and drug development (Saklayen, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Asprosin is the C-terminal cleavage product of profibrillin encoded by FBN1.
source: we recently discovered a fasting-induced, glucogenic, and orexigenic hormone that is the C-terminal cleavage product of profibrillin (encoded by FBN1) and named it asprosin (Romere et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to the original discovery paper.

claim: Asprosin's two major sites of action are the liver and the brain.
source: Its two major sites of action are the liver and the brain (Romere et al., 2016; Li et al., 2019; Duerrschmid et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to supporting research.

claim: At the liver, asprosin causes a glucogenic effect through a cAMP-PKA-dependent pathway.
source: At the liver, asprosin causes a glucogenic effect through a cAMP-PKA-dependent pathway (Romere et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Asprosin promotes hepatic glucose release through the binding of OR4M1, an olfactory G-coupled protein receptor in the rhodopsin family.
source: It was found recently to promote hepatic glucose release through the binding of OR4M1, an olfactory G-coupled protein receptor in the rhodopsin family (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to recent research.

claim: Asprosin binds the mouse ortholog Olfr734 with high affinity.
source: In addition, asprosin was shown to bind the mouse ortholog, Olfr734 with high affinity, and elimination of the receptor considerably reduced the glucogenic effects of exogenously administered asprosin (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Elimination of Olfr734 considerably reduced the glucogenic effects of exogenously administered asprosin.
source: In addition, asprosin was shown to bind the mouse ortholog, Olfr734 with high affinity, and elimination of the receptor considerably reduced the glucogenic effects of exogenously administered asprosin (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Asprosin crosses the blood brain barrier and exerts effects on the hypothalamus.
source: There is also evidence, that asprosin crosses the blood brain barrier and exerts effects on the hypothalamus (Duerrschmid et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: In the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, asprosin directly activates orexigenic AgRP neurons and indirectly inhibits anorexigenic POMC neurons, resulting in appetite stimulation.
source: In the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus, asprosin directly activates orexigenic AgRP neurons and indirectly inhibits anorexigenic POMC neurons, resulting in appetite stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing asprosin's mechanism of action in the brain.

claim: Patients with NPS present with low appetite associated with extreme leanness and robust insulin sensitivity.
source: Patients with NPS, a human genetic model of deficiency in plasma asprosin, present with low appetite associated with extreme leanness and robust insulin sensitivity (Romere et al., 2016; Duerrschmid et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations.

claim: NPS mutations in mice (Fbn1NPS/+) result in phenocopy of the human disorder.
source: NPS mutations in mice (Fbn1NPS/+) result in phenocopy of the human disorder, and depressed AgRP neuron activity, which can be restored to normal with asprosin replenishment in vivo and ex vivo (Duerrschmid et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Fbn1NPS/+ mice are completely immune to diet-induced MS.
source: Importantly, Fbn1NPS/+ mice are completely immune to diet-induced MS (Duerrschmid et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation.

claim: Patients and mice with MS exhibit elevated plasma asprosin.
source: On the opposite end of the energy-balance spectrum, patients and mice with MS exhibit elevated plasma asprosin (Duerrschmid et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020a; Ugur and Aydin, 2019; Alan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2019; Baykus et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations.

claim: A cohort of adult men with MS have significantly elevated plasma asprosin, with levels more than twofold higher than those of unaffected age- and sex-matched individuals.
source: Here we find that a cohort of adult men with MS have significantly elevated plasma asprosin, with levels more than twofold higher than those of unaffected age- and sex-matched individuals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: A single dose of an asprosin-neutralizing mAb significantly reduced food intake by an average of 1 g/day in DIO mice.
source: A single dose of an asprosin-neutralizing mAb was sufficient to significantly reduce food intake by an average of 1 g/day in the treatment group, but not in mice receiving a control, isotype-matched IgG (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1a.

claim: The decrease in food intake after a single dose of anti-asprosin mAb was associated with a 0.7 g average reduction in body weight over 24 hr in DIO mice.
source: This decrease in food intake was associated with a 0.7 g average reduction in body weight over 24 hr (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1b.

claim: In fasted DIO mice, a significant blood glucose reduction was evident as early as 2 hr post-mAb treatment, with the effect most pronounced at 4 hr and 6 hr after injection.
source: In mice without access to food, a significant blood glucose reduction was evident as early as 2 hr post-mAb treatment. The effect was most pronounced at 4 hr and 6 hr after injection (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1c.

claim: Decreased blood glucose after mAb treatment was not paralleled by increased glucosuria.
source: Importantly, decreased blood glucose was not paralleled by increased glucosuria in response to mAb treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), ruling glucosuria out as a potential mechanism for blood glucose reduction.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The blood glucose lowering effect of anti-asprosin mAb is independent of reductions in food intake.
source: Also, given that mice were without access to food, this result demonstrates that the blood glucose lowering effect is independent of reductions in food intake.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the experimental design where mice were fasted.

claim: In lean C57BL/6 mice, anti-asprosin mAb showed a subtle effect on blood glucose without inducing hypoglycemia, and no effect on 24 hr cumulative food intake or body weight.
source: Interestingly, repeating this experiment in lean C57BL/6 mice (with normal plasma asprosin compared with DIO mice) showed a subtle effect on blood glucose without inducing hypoglycemia, and no effect at all on 24 hr cumulative food intake or body weight (Figure 1—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Elevation in plasma asprosin or presence of florid MS may be necessary prerequisites to unlocking the full therapeutic effect of asprosin neutralization.
source: suggesting that elevation in plasma asprosin or presence of florid MS may be necessary prerequisites to unlocking the full therapeutic effect of asprosin neutralization.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the differential effects in lean vs. DIO mice.

claim: NPS (Fbn1NPS/+) mice were completely unresponsive to mAb treatment, with no effect on blood glucose, 24 hr cumulative food intake, and body weight.
source: Furthermore, NPS (Fbn1NPS/+) mice, with genetic loss of asprosin, were completely unresponsive to mAb treatment, with no effect at all on blood glucose, 24 hr cumulative food intake, and body weight (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The glucose and appetite reducing actions of the anti-asprosin mAb are specifically due to asprosin neutralization, and not potential off-target or toxic effects.
source: These results again suggest that the glucose and appetite reducing actions of this particular anti-asprosin mAb are specifically due to asprosin neutralization, and not potential off-target or toxic effects.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the NPS mouse data.

claim: Markers of general sickness, plasma levels of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines, and markers of renal and hepatic health were unaltered in DIO mice treated with the anti-asprosin mAb.
source: Markers of general sickness (pedestrian locomotor and intentional wheel running activity), plasma levels of pro-inflammatory (IL1β and TNFα) and anti-inflammatory (IL10 and TGFβ) cytokines, markers of renal (plasma creatinine and BUN), and hepatic health (plasma ALT, alanine aminotransferase and AST, aspartate aminotransferase) were unaltered in DIO mice treated with the anti-asprosin mAb (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), suggesting lack of a broad toxicity signature.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: A single dose of anti-asprosin mAb resulted in a significant reduction in blood glucose levels, plasma insulin and triglyceride levels, and 24 hr cumulative food intake and body weight in a dose-dependent manner in DIO mice.
source: A single dose of the mAb resulted in a significant reduction in blood glucose levels (measured 4 hr post-treatment), in plasma insulin and triglyceride levels (measured 24 hr post-treatment), and in 24 hr cumulative food intake and body weight in a dose-dependent manner in DIO mice (Figure 2a–e).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Half maximal inhibitor concentration (IC50) for blood glucose, insulin, and triglycerides was in the range of 30–55 µg/mouse (~1.5 mg/kg).
source: Half maximal inhibitor concentration (IC50) determined using four-parameter non-linear variable slope curve for these three measures was in the range of 30–55 µg/mouse (~1.5 mg/kg).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on dose-response analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mice transduced with Ad5-FBN1, Ad5-Asprosin, and AAV8-Asprosin all exhibited hyperphagia, gained weight, and displayed significantly higher baseline glucose and insulin levels compared to control mice.
source: When compared to mice transduced with Ad5-empty and AAV8-empty control viral vectors, mice transduced with Ad5-FBN1, Ad5-Asprosin, and AAV8-Asprosin all exhibited hyperphagia, gained weight, and displayed significantly higher baseline glucose and insulin levels (Figure 3a,e,i; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–d,f–i,k–n; Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3 and supplementary figures.

claim: The metabolic phenotype in viral overexpression experiments was coincident with the elevation of human asprosin in mouse plasma.
source: This metabolic phenotype in all three experiments was coincident with the elevation of human asprosin in mouse plasma in the time it takes to achieve peak expression in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e,j,o; Crystal, 2014; Zincarelli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: When injected with anti-asprosin mAb, mice with viral overexpression of human asprosin restored their food intake back to normal.
source: When injected with the anti-asprosin mAb, mice with viral overexpression of human asprosin restored their food intake back to normal (Figure 3b,f,j)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Anti-asprosin mAb treatment resulted in an average net body weight loss of 0.3–0.5 g within the first 24 hr in mice with viral overexpression of asprosin.
source: and this resulted in an average net body weight loss of 0.3–0.5 g within the first 24 hr (Figure 3c,g,k).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: A single injection of anti-asprosin mAb reduced baseline glucose levels back to normal in mice with viral overexpression of asprosin.
source: A single injection of mouse anti-asprosin mAb also reduced baseline glucose levels back to normal (Figure 3d,h,i).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: In DIO mice treated with daily injection for 10 days, a ~10% decrease in body weight was observed with asprosin neutralization.
source: In DIO mice treated with daily injection for 10 days, we observed a ~10% decrease in body weight with asprosin neutralization (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4a.

claim: The body weight reduction after 10 days of mAb treatment was associated with improved glucose tolerance on day 11.
source: that was associated with improved glucose tolerance on day 11 (after 1 day without mAb) (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4b.

claim: On day 13 (10 days of mAb treatment followed by 3 days without mAb), the body weight difference remained the same but the improved glucose tolerance disappeared.
source: On day 13 however (10 days of once daily mAb treatment followed by 3 days without mAb treatment), the body weight difference between the two groups remained the same (Figure 4c), but the improved glucose tolerance disappeared (Figure 4d)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4c-d.

claim: The effect of asprosin neutralization on glucose homeostasis is independent of systemic improvements in metabolism due to weight loss.
source: showing once again that the effect of asprosin neutralization on glucose homeostasis is independent of systemic improvements in metabolism due to weight loss
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the day 13 data.

claim: The anti-asprosin mAb has a short effect-life of 24–48 hr.
source: and also demonstrating the short effect-life of the mAb (24–48 hr).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the loss of glucose tolerance improvement by day 13.

claim: A 14 day course of daily injection of anti-asprosin mAb significantly reduced food intake and body weight in DIO mice, Leprdb/db mice, and mice on AMLN diet.
source: A 14 day course of daily injection of an anti-asprosin mAb significantly reduced food intake and body weight in diet-induced MS (DIO mice; Figure 4e,f; Figure 4—figure supplement 1a; Figure 4—figure supplement 2a,c,d), genetic MS (Leprdb/db mice; Figure 4i,j; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), as well as in mice on a diet rich in fructose and cholesterol in addition to fat (AMLN diet) (Figure 4m,n; Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4 and supplementary figures.

claim: Mice treated with anti-asprosin mAb for 14 days weighed approximately 5–11% less than mice treated with a control mAb.
source: On average, mice treated with the mAb weighed approximately 5–11% less than mice treated with a control mAb
evidence: This is stated in the results section summarizing the 14-day treatment data.

claim: The reduction in body weight and food intake in response to 14 day mAb treatment in DIO mice was coincident with a reduction in subcutaneous and visceral fat depots, with no effect on lean mass.
source: The reduction in body weight and food intake in response to 14 day mAb treatment in DIO mice was coincident with a reduction in subcutaneous and visceral fat depots, with no effect observed on lean mass (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by MRI data in Figure 5.

claim: All three mouse models of MS displayed improvement in hyperglycemia after 14 days of mAb treatment.
source: Furthermore, while all three mouse models of MS displayed improvement in hyperglycemia (Figure 4g,k,o)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: A significant reduction in plasma insulin after 14 days of mAb treatment was observed only in DIO mice.
source: a significant reduction in plasma insulin after mAb treatment was observed only in DIO mice (Figure 4h,l,p).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: A single injection of anti-asprosin mAb significantly reduced plasma levels of total cholesterol, LDL, glycerol, and triglycerides in DIO mice.
source: A single injection of the anti-asprosin mAb significantly reduced plasma levels of total cholesterol, LDL, glycerol, and triglycerides in DIO mice, measured 6 hr after injection in mice without access to food (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a–f).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Chronic treatment for 2 weeks in DIO, Leprdb/db, and AMLN diet-treated mice did not display uniform improvements in plasma lipids despite marked improvements in appetite, body weight, and plasma glucose levels.
source: Chronic treatment for 2 weeks however, in DIO, Leprdb/db, and AMLN diet-treated mice, did not display the uniform improvements in plasma lipids that were noted with a single injection, despite marked improvements in appetite, body weight, and plasma glucose levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 3g–x).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: A single injection of each of the three mAbs (mouse, rabbit, and human) resulted in significantly improved glucose tolerance in DIO mice.
source: A single injection of each of the three mAbs resulted in significantly improved glucose tolerance (Figure 6a)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6a.

claim: A single injection of each of the three mAbs resulted in a reduction in food intake and body weight in DIO mice.
source: and a reduction in food intake (Figure 6b) and body weight (Figure 6c) in DIO mice.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6b-c.

claim: The mouse and human mAbs compete for binding to asprosin and recognize the same or an overlapping epitope.
source: Of these three mAbs, the mouse and human mAbs compete for binding to asprosin and so recognize the same or an overlapping epitope
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by epitope competition data in Figure 6d.

claim: The rabbit mAb recognizes a distinct epitope from the mouse and human mAbs, displaying no binding competition.
source: whereas the rabbit mAb recognizes a distinct epitope, displaying no binding competition (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by epitope competition data in Figure 6d.

claim: The positive metabolic effects of asprosin neutralization are epitope-agnostic.
source: This indicates that, insofar as these two epitopes are concerned, the positive metabolic effects of asprosin neutralization are epitope-agnostic.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the multi-mAb data.

claim: In DIO mice, the free mouse anti-asprosin mAb had a half-life of approximately 11 days.
source: In DIO mice, the free mouse anti-asprosin mAb had the longest half-life, of approximately 11 days
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on pharmacokinetic measurements shown in Figure 6e.

claim: In DIO mice, the free rabbit anti-asprosin mAb had a half-life of approximately 5.6 days.
source: the free rabbit anti-asprosin mAb had a half-life of approximately 5.6 days
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on pharmacokinetic measurements shown in Figure 6f.

claim: In DIO mice, the free human anti-asprosin mAb had a half-life of approximately 3.2 days.
source: and the free human anti-asprosin mAb had a half-life of approximately 3.2 days.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on pharmacokinetic measurements shown in Figure 6g.

claim: The half-lives of the three mAbs were fairly similar in Fbn1NPS/+ mice, indicating that the concentration of circulating asprosin does not appear to directly influence the rate of mAb clearance.
source: Of note, the half-lives of these three mAbs were fairly similar in Fbn1NPS/+ mice, indicating that the concentration of circulating asprosin does not appear to directly influence the rate of mAb clearance.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the pharmacokinetic data.

claim: The affinity (KD) of the rabbit mAb to recombinant human asprosin was calculated as <10 pM.
source: The affinity (KD) of the rabbit mAb to recombinant human asprosin was calculated as <10 pM from a kon of 1.11 × 105 M−1s−1 and a koff <1×10−7 s−1 (r2 = 0.99, χ2 = 99.88).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on binding affinity measurements shown in Figure 6h.

claim: The mouse mAb displayed a KD of 0.48 ± 0.02 nM.
source: The mouse mAb displayed a KD of 0.48 ± 0.02 nM with kon of (1.45 ± 0.003) × 105 M−1s−1 and koff of (6.67 ± 0.23) × 10−5 s−1 (r2 = 0.99, χ2 = 15.05).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on binding affinity measurements shown in Figure 6i.

claim: The human mAb displayed a KD of 14.4 ± 0.24 nM.
source: The human mAb displayed a KD of 14.4 ± 0.24 nM with kon of (6.76 ± 0.07) × 104 M−1s−1 and koff of (9.71 ± 0.13) × 10−4 s−1 (r2 = 0.94, χ2 = 408.8).
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on binding affinity measurements shown in Figure 6j.

claim: The rabbit mAb has the highest affinity for asprosin and the human mAb the lowest, over a 1000-fold range.
source: Thus, the rabbit mAb has the highest affinity for asprosin and the human mAb the lowest, over a 1000-fold range.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a summary of the binding affinity data.

claim: All three mAbs were able to functionally neutralize asprosin in vivo despite differences in affinity.
source: Nevertheless, all three mAbs were able to functionally neutralize asprosin in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the functional studies.

claim: The rabbit and fully human anti-asprosin mAbs reversibly and completely inhibited recombinant asprosin's activating effect on AgRP+ neuron firing frequency and membrane potential.
source: Similar to previously published effects of the mouse anti-asprosin mAb on AgRP+ neurons (Duerrschmid et al., 2017), the rabbit and fully human anti-asprosin mAbs reversibly and completely inhibited recombinant asprosin's activating effect on AgRP+neuron firing frequency and membrane potential (Figure 7a–f).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by electrophysiology data in Figure 7a-f.

claim: A single injection of each of the three mAbs resulted in significant reduction in hepatic cAMP levels in fasting DIO mice.
source: Furthermore, a single injection of each of the three mAbs resulted in significant reduction in hepatic cAMP levels in fasting DIO mice (Figure 7g,h).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7g-h.

claim: All three anti-asprosin mAbs have potent neutralizing activity against exogenous and endogenous asprosin at the level of both its orexigenic and glucogenic functions.
source: These results indicate potent neutralizing activity of all three anti-asprosin mAbs against exogenous and endogenous asprosin, and at the level of both its functions (orexigenic and glucogenic).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the mechanistic studies.

claim: Four outside groups have replicated asprosin's physiological effects in vivo.
source: To underscore this point, four outside groups have by now replicated asprosin's physiological effects in vivo (Li et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2020; Hekim, 2021; Zhang et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to independent replication studies.

claim: Outside groups have expanded asprosin biology beyond the original discoveries, including modulation of muscle AMPK, identification of the liver asprosin receptor OR4M1, identification of a new asprosin-like hormone derived from FBN2 (placensin).
source: and also expanded asprosin biology beyond our discoveries (modulation of muscle AMPK, identification of the liver asprosin receptor OR4M1, identification of a new asprosin-like hormone derived from FBN2, placensin).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion describing independent research that has built on the original asprosin discovery.

claim: Asprosin neutralization resulted in reduced food intake and a parallel reduction in body weight and adipose mass in mice on a high-fat diet (DIO mice).
source: Asprosin neutralization resulted in reduced food intake and a parallel reduction in body weight and adipose mass in mice on a high-fat diet (DIO mice).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the results.

claim: A similar hypophagic and body weight reduction phenotype was seen in mice on the AMLN diet and mice with a genetic loss of leptin signaling (Leprdb/db).
source: A similar hypophagic and body weight reduction phenotype was also seen in more severe preclinical models of MS, such as mice on the AMLN diet and mice with a genetic loss of leptin signaling (Leprdb/db).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of the results.

claim: Asprosin neutralization is effective independent of leptin and opens therapeutic avenues for a wide range of cases of hyperphagia and obesity.
source: These results indicate that asprosin neutralization is effective independent of leptin and opens therapeutic avenues for a wide range of cases of hyperphagia and obesity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the results in leptin-deficient mice.

claim: The direction of improvement in response to asprosin neutralization was dependent on the stage and phase of MS.
source: Furthermore, the direction of improvement in response to asprosin neutralization was dependent on the stage and phase of MS.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on observations in different age groups of mice.

claim: Younger Leprdb/db mice (12 weeks of age) in the linear phase of body weight increase were protected from weight gain upon asprosin neutralization.
source: Younger Leprdb/db mice, while still in the linear phase of body weight increase (12 weeks of age) (Wang et al., 2020b), were protected from weight gain upon asprosin neutralization.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: Older Leprdb/db mice (30 weeks of age) that have reached the plateaued weight phase lost weight in response to asprosin neutralization.
source: On the other hand, older Leprdb/db mice that have reached the plateaued weight phase (30 weeks of age) (Wang et al., 2020b) lost weight in response to asprosin neutralization.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: mAb-mediated improvements in hyperglycemia were independent of change in food intake.
source: Additionally, mAb-mediated improvements in hyperglycemia were independent of change in food intake given that mice were without access to food.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the fasting experiments.

claim: A low IC50 of 30–55 µg/mouse (~1.5 mg/kg) was determined for the four key features of MS (hyperphagia, obesity, hyperglycemia, and hypertriglyceridemia).
source: Furthermore, a low IC50 of 30–55 µg/mouse (~1.5 mg/kg) was determined for the four key features of MS (hyperphagia, obesity, hyperglycemia, and hypertriglyceridemia).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the dose-response results.

claim: The low IC50 highlights the pharmacological inhibitory potency of asprosin neutralization for MS in its entirety.
source: The low IC50, well within the spectrum of acceptable therapeutic mAb dosing, highlights the pharmacological inhibitory potency of asprosin neutralization for MS in its entirety, rather than improving only a particular manifestation of it (Strik et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation.

claim: The effect of escalating dose on appetite reduction is linear, but exhibits a defined upper and lower threshold for improvement of other attributes of MS such as blood glucose, insulin, triglycerides, and body weight.
source: While the effect of escalating dose on appetite reduction is linear, it exhibits a defined upper and lower threshold when it comes to improvement of other attributes of MS such as blood glucose, insulin, triglycerides, and body weight.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the dose-response curve shapes.

claim: The plateauing of mAb effect at higher doses may indicate arrival at a physiological equilibrium state and the impact of compensatory mechanisms.
source: This may indicate arrival at a physiological equilibrium state and the impact of compensatory mechanisms to prevent further, potentially disastrous changes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as speculation about the dose-response plateau.

claim: mAb treatment did not result in any changes in lean euglycemic WT mice except for a short-lived reduction in blood glucose without crossing over into overt hypoglycemia.
source: Interestingly, mAb treatment did not result in any changes in lean euglycemic WT mice except for a short-lived reduction in blood glucose (without crossing over into overt hypoglycemia).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the lean mouse results.

claim: The dependence of anti-asprosin mAb therapeutics on high endogenous asprosin levels portends a strong safety profile.
source: These results suggest the dependence of anti-asprosin mAb therapeutics on high endogenous asprosin levels and portends a strong safety profile.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the differential effects in lean vs. obese mice.

claim: A strong safety profile and high specificity of anti-asprosin mAbs is reiterated by the complete lack of a response to mAb treatment in Fbn1NPS/+ mice.
source: A strong safety profile and high specificity of anti-asprosin mAbs is reiterated by the complete lack of a response to mAb treatment in Fbn1NPS/+ mice that display little circulating asprosin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the NPS mouse results.
